title: Property tax exemption for Veterans with disabilities
summary: Oregon exempts part of the assessed value of your home if you are rated 40 percent or more disabled. There are two tiers, and the exempt amount rises by 3 percent every year, so ask your county assessor for this year's figure.
amount: Two tiers of assessed value, each increasing by 3 percent a year. Get the current year's dollar figure from your county assessor.
eligibility: You are a Veteran as defined in ORS 408.225, and you own and live in the homestead
Higher tier: the VA or a branch of service has certified service-connected disabilities of 40 percent or more
Lower tier: the VA or a branch has certified disabilities of 40 percent or more, without the service-connected requirement

Lower tier alternative: one licensed physician or naturopathic physician certifies you are rated 40 percent or more disabled, but only if your total gross income last calendar year was not more than 185 percent of the federal poverty guidelines
An unremarried surviving spouse of a Veteran qualifies for the lower tier, for the period before any first remarriage

An unremarried surviving spouse qualifies for the higher tier if the Veteran died from a service-connected injury or illness, or the Veteran received at least one year of the maximum higher-tier exemption after 1981
details: We are deliberately not publishing a current dollar figure here. The statute sets base amounts of $15,000 of assessed value for the lower tier and $18,000 for the service-connected tier, but it then provides that the exemption each year equals 103 percent of the prior tax year's exemption. The statute gives no starting year and no current figure, so any number we printed would be wrong within a year. The index is the thing to know: 3 percent, compounding, every year.
Your county assessor holds the current year's amount. Ask for it directly rather than working from a figure you read anywhere, including here.

File a written claim with the county assessor, on the assessor's form, on or before 1 April of the assessment year. If you acquired the property after 1 March and before 1 July, file within 30 days of acquiring it.
If you miss 1 April the assessor notifies you by 10 April, and you can still apply up to 1 May with a $10 late filing fee.

Most claimants do not refile each year. If the exemption was allowed last year, you still qualify under the same paragraph, and ownership and use have not changed, no new claim is needed. The exception is the physician-certified low-income route, which does have to be filed annually.

A VA or branch certificate has to be dated within three years. A physician certificate has to be dated within one year and comes with a sworn statement of total gross income. Every claim needs an affidavit.
The certificate requirement does not apply if you filed one after turning 65, or if you filed a certificate of a permanent rating on or after 27 September 1987.

A surviving spouse can elect to continue the exemption without a new claim where the Veteran died in the previous tax year, or where the homestead was acquired after 1 March and before 1 July and the Veteran died within 30 days of acquiring it. Notify the assessor. Taxes already paid are refunded and unpaid taxes abated.

If your federal certification of 40 percent or more disability arrives late, ORS 307.262 lets you claim for each tax year after the certified date, provided you file within six months of the federal notice and go back no more than three tax years.

title: Military pay subtraction, which does not cover retirement pay
summary: Oregon subtracts certain military pay from your income, but read this one carefully: the statute defines military pay to exclude retirement pay and pensions. Military retirement does not qualify.
amount: Varies by category of service. Service not falling into a named category is capped at $6,000 a year.
eligibility: Pay for service performed outside Oregon in the year of your initial draft or enlistment, or in the year of your discharge

Pay for service performed outside Oregon in any month beginning on or after 1 August 1990 and before the date the President designated as the end of combatant activities in the Persian Gulf Desert Shield area
Reserve component pay, where you were away from home overnight, were required to be away, and the duty lasted at least 21 consecutive days, which need not fall in the same tax year
Pay for an Oregon National Guard member in active state service or state active duty under ORS 396.005
Any other military pay not covered by those categories, up to $6,000 a year
details: The important catch sits in the definition. The statute defines military pay as pay for active duty, inactive duty, training and reserve component duty including state active duty, and any other compensation other than retirement pay or pension. Military retirement pay and pensions are therefore outside this subtraction entirely.
The total subtraction cannot exceed your total military pay included in federal taxable income for the year.
The $6,000 figure for the catch-all category is flat in the text. No inflation adjustment is written into it.
This subtraction lives in ORS 316.792, not in the main modification section at ORS 316.680, which has no military provision. If you are looking it up yourself, go straight to 316.792.
Amendments made in 2023 apply to tax years beginning on or after 1 January 2021.
